1.title: Authentication, Authorization and Integration Protocols
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Authentication, Authorization and Integration Protocols. This module covers authentication, authorization and integration protocols. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Authentication versus authorization in a Claude system. How to spot security gaps in an integration. OAuth two point one for M C P (Model Context Protocol): roles, P K C E, audience, scopes. Choosing M C P, A P I (application programming interface) or C L I (command-line interface) or agent-to-agent.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Reviews a Healthcare Client's Records Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Reviews a Healthcare Client's Records Assistant. The assistant reads patient records through one shared service account with access to every record. A clinician asks about "my patients", yet the model could return any patient's chart. The A P I key sits in a mobile app.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization
1.text: Authentication and Authorization. Authentication equals who is calling. Authorization equals what that identity may do. The model is never the access-control layer: it can be persuaded; code cannot.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization, continued
1.text: Authentication and Authorization, continued. The figure shows this: Identity must reach the tool and the data system: the application authenticates the user, passes their identity to the tool, and the data system enforces that user's permissions, not the model.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization, continued
1.text: Authentication and Authorization, continued. Shared service credential for all users. Why it is a problem: Every user acts with the broadest access; no per-user audit. Fix: Propagate the end user's identity; use delegated tokens and the user's permissions. Authorization in the prompt ("only show the user's records"). Why it is a problem: Can be bypassed by injection or error. Fix: Enforce in the tool or data layer. Over-broad scopes or roles. Why it is a problem: Larger blast radius. Fix: Least-privilege scopes; split read and write. Long-lived tokens. Why it is a problem: Theft window. Fix: Short-lived tokens, refresh, rotation. Secrets in client code or prompts. Why it is a problem: Leak risk. Fix: Server-side secrets manager; environment variables; never in the browser or mobile app.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization, continued
1.text: Authentication and Authorization, continued. No audit trail. Why it is a problem: Cannot investigate. Fix: Log identity, tool, arguments, result. Tools with destructive actions. Why it is a problem: Injection impact. Fix: Remove, or gate with human approval. Token passthrough. Why it is a problem: Confused-deputy risk. Fix: Server accepts only tokens issued for it. A P I keys: start with sk-ant-, are shown once, belong in a secrets manager, are read from an environment variable, should have expiry and be scoped to a workspace or service account; never ship them in browser or mobile code. Route calls through your back end.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization, continued
1.text: Authentication and Authorization, continued. Organizations on zero data retention cannot call the A P I from a browser at all (cross-origin calls are rejected). Exam tip: "Which control closes the gap?" Usually enforce the user's permissions in code at the tool or data layer with the real identity, not a stronger prompt and not a bigger model.

1.title: OAuth 2.1 and MCP
1.text: OAuth two point one and M C P. The figure shows this: M C P authorization roles: client, M C P server as resource server, authorization server, and the user's browser for consent.

1.title: OAuth 2.1 and MCP, continued
1.text: OAuth two point one and M C P, continued. Scope. Authorization is optional in M C P; for H T T P transports follow the spec (OAuth two point one); S T D I O servers should not use it and read credentials from the environment. Roles. M C P server equals resource server; M C P client equals OAuth client; separate authorization server. Discovery. Servers publish protected resource metadata; clients discover the authorization server. P K C E. Clients protect the authorization-code flow with P K C E. Resource parameter. Client sends the server's canonical U R I so the token is bound to it. Audience validation. The server must verify the token was issued for it.

1.title: OAuth 2.1 and MCP, continued
1.text: OAuth two point one and M C P, continued. No passthrough. Servers must not accept or forward tokens meant for other services; clients send only tokens from the server's own authorization server. Transport. Authorization: Bearer header on every request; never in the U R L (uniform resource locator). Scopes. Request the minimum; the server's challenge names required scopes; four hundred three insufficient scope triggers step-up with the union of scopes. Status codes. four hundred one missing or invalid token; four hundred three insufficient scope; four hundred malformed request. Client registration. Client I D metadata documents preferred; pre-registration; dynamic registration is deprecated.

1.title: OAuth 2.1 and MCP, continued
1.text: OAuth two point one and M C P, continued. Confused deputy: a server that forwards the user's token to a downstream A P I (or accepts any token) can be tricked into acting with authority it should not hold. Custom connectors reach servers over the public internet and the user must trust the server; only connect servers you trust. Skills and hooks can add deterministic checks around tool calls (Module thirteen).

1.title: Choosing the Integration Mechanism
1.text: Choosing the Integration Mechanism. The figure shows this: Choosing an integration mechanism: direct A P I or C L I for simple owned integrations, M C P for reusable tool and data capabilities, agent-to-agent for delegating to separate agents.

1.title: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued
1.text: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued. Direct A P I or C L I. What it is: Your code (or a shell tool) calls a service. Use when: Simple, one-off, fully owned, stable interface. Watch for: Duplicated glue per app; each tool schema maintained separately. M C P. What it is: Open protocol connecting an agent to tools, data and prompts. Use when: A capability shared by several applications, maintained independently; a catalog of tools. Watch for: Server trust, auth setup, tool bloat.

1.title: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued
1.text: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued. A to A (agent-to-agent). What it is: Open protocol for agents to discover and delegate to other agents, across frameworks, staying opaque. Use when: A separate agent owned by another team or vendor must be called as a peer. Watch for: Not a tool-call or S D K (software development kit) substitute; adds a network boundary. M C P and A to A are complementary: an agent uses M C P for its tools and A to A to collaborate with other agents. C L I tools (for example git, kubectl) can be the simplest integration for coding agents, with permission rules around them.

1.title: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued
1.text: Choosing the Integration Mechanism, continued. Prefer M C P when the same capability serves multiple agents or applications, or when an existing server already exists; prefer direct A P I when it is a single app and the interface is small. Exam tip: Authorization belongs in code with the real user identity; a shared service credential loses per-user permissions and audit. Exam tip: M C P servers must check the token audience and must never pass tokens through; tokens never go in the U R L.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Auth N versus Auth Z: Who versus what; enforce Auth Z in code, never in the model. Gaps: Shared credentials, prompt-based authorization, broad scopes, long-lived tokens, secrets client-side, no audit, destructive tools. A P I keys: sk-ant-, shown once, secrets manager, server-side only, expiry. M C P auth: Optional; H T T P equals OAuth two point one; S T D I O equals environment; P K C E; resource parameter; audience check; no passthrough. Codes: four hundred one token; four hundred three insufficient scope (step-up); four hundred malformed. Choose: Direct A P I or C L I simple and owned; M C P reusable tools and data; A to A delegate to separate agents.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A records assistant uses one shared service account that can read every patient chart. Which change best fixes the gap? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Authorization must be enforced in code with the real identity; prompts and logs do not prevent access.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A mobile app calls the Claude A P I directly with a key embedded in the app. What is the right design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A key shipped to clients is a leaked key; keep it server-side.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An M C P server receives a token issued for a different service and passes it to a downstream A P I. Which principle is violated? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Servers must accept only tokens issued for them and must not forward others (confused deputy).

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An M C P server returns four hundred three with error insufficient scope and a scope for write access. What should a well-behaved client do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Step-up requests the needed scopes, preserving earlier ones, and limits retries.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two are correct about M C P authorization? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. Audience validation is required; transport determines the mechanism; tokens never go in U R L s.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Three internal applications need the same C R M lookup and update capability, maintained by the C R M team. Which integration is most appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A reusable, independently maintained capability is the M C P use case.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A claims agent must hand a fraud-scoring task to an agent operated by a vendor using a different framework. Which mechanism fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A to A is for agents collaborating across owners and frameworks.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: A. Question two: A. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: C and D. Question six: B. Question seven: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
